> 謙。亨。君子有終。

謙 is the most quietly mistranslated character in the book, and the problem is structural.

## 謙 is 從言，兼聲

說文: 謙，敬也。從言，兼聲.

It is a phonetic compound. 言 is the semantic side; 兼 is the sound.

The tempting reading is to take it as a picture: words (言) plus holding two things at once (兼), therefore "speaking without claiming fullness." It is a good sentence. It is not the character.

This is the same class of error as 訟's 從言公聲 — the third one this book has had to correct. Easy readings lose to correct ones, and 謙 is where the loss is most costly, because the pleasing reading turns a discipline into a manner of speech.

## 兼 is a hand holding two grain stalks

說文: 兼，并也。從又持秝 — 又 is the hand, 秝 is two stalks of grain.

So 兼's original sense is "together, holding both at once."

But the dictionary's gloss for 謙 is 敬 — reverent, circumspect, not treating oneself lightly.

So the "not full of oneself" layer is an extension from the components, defensible as interpretation and not the original sense. The word itself says: reverence.

Which is a colder and more demanding instruction than modesty. Modesty is a manner; 敬 is an attention that does not slacken.

## 謙謙

Line 1: 謙謙君子，用涉大川，吉.

Reverence upon reverence — not one act of deferring, but a constant holding.

And the same line crosses the great river. Which is the first of the chapter's inversions: the posture that looks like weakness is the one that gets across.

## 鳴謙

Line 2: 鳴謙，貞吉.

鳴 is to sound abroad. The reverence has become audible; people know about it.

And the judgement is still 吉, because the line's caution is not about being known. It is about whether being known changes anything. Line 2 keeps it.

## 勞謙

Line 3: 勞謙君子，有終，吉.

勞 is merit, work accomplished.

Reverence after having accomplished something.

The chapter flags this as the hardest layer — 無功而謙容易，有功而謙極難. Being unassuming when you have nothing to be assuming about costs nothing. The hexagram puts its 有終 on this line, not on the first one.

## 㧑謙

Line 4: 無不利，㧑謙.

說文: 㧑，裂也 — to split, to divide; thence to scatter, to distribute.

So 㧑謙 is distributing one's own gains and reputation outward.

Reverence that has become an action: not holding back from credit, but pushing the credit away from oneself and toward others.

## 裒多益寡，稱物平施

The 象: take from the abundant to add to the scant; weigh the things, then distribute evenly.

And the order inside those four characters is the whole argument. 稱 first, 平 after.

Weigh, then level. To level without weighing is egalitarianism — equal shares regardless of the object. To weigh and then level is the governance the hexagram is describing.

平 is not "the same amount for everyone." It is each thing getting what its weight calls for. Which is why the sentence needs the scale before the distribution.

## The test

Take a piece of credit you recently received. Ask which of the four lines you are in: holding back before you had anything (1), being seen to be restrained (2), restrained after a real accomplishment (3), or actively pushing the credit out (4). The hexagram orders them by difficulty, and the difficulty is not in the first.
